content:
Inferno Games keeps track of the games I own, what I’m playing now, and my backlog. It pulls in my whole Steam library and splits playtime between my Windows PC and my Steam Deck.
The library # The game library Every game I’m tracking # Games I’m tracking each get a card with their status (backlog, playing, completed, on hold or dropped), the platform, the developer and year, and how long I’ve played. Some cards also carry a DLC tag.
Filters cover status, platform and genre, with favorites and a few ways to sort.
A game's page, with playtime by device A page per game # Each game has its own page. For Steam games, it shows the playtime split between Windows and Steam Deck, synced from Steam, next to the buttons to change its status.
The Steam side # My Steam library, sorted by playtime Steam Library # Every game on my Steam account, enriched with data from IGDB. It can sort by playtime or by when I last played, filter played and unplayed games, and add any of them to the backlog in one click.
Steam stats Steam Stats # The big picture: 394 games, about 11,000 hours in total, and how much of the library I’ve actually played.
The platform breakdown shows my top games on PC and on the Deck, and a filter can drop the outliers with thousands of hours so they don’t swamp everything else.
title: Inferno Games: My Game Library, Backlog and Steam Stats

content:
After I made the Season 2 Rewind mod I wanted it to work with the Telltale Mod Launcher, the launcher the Telltale Modding Group uses for The Walking Dead Definitive Series. Its last release was 0.6.5. It was a .NET Framework 4.7.2 WPF app, and it depended on a LibTelltale.dll that was never in the repo, so it couldn’t build from a clean clone.
So I forked it and rebuilt it. Credit for the original goes to David Matos (frostbone25) and the Telltale Modding Group.
Fork and release on GitHub
What changed # The redesigned library, from the pull request The new launcher is .NET 10 with Avalonia, so the same code runs on Windows and Linux. A Steam copy of the game on Linux is started through Steam, so it runs under Proton.
Your games sit in a sidebar. The selected game shows at the top with its own icon, read straight out of its exe, and Steam’s cached artwork behind the title. Drop a mod’s zip anywhere on the window to install it. You can set up more than one game. Light and dark themes. The code is split into a core library with no UI in it (settings, Steam lookup, install, scan and remove) and the Avalonia app on top. There are 87 tests, including headless render tests that draw every window with the real styles.
The bugs that were losing mods # The upstream repo had two open issues: mods disappearing after a restart, and a mod that installed but did nothing. Reading the 0.6.5 code turned up four causes:
A file watcher race The old launcher rescanned Archives whenever a .json appeared and deleted any mod with missing files. Graphic Black Disabler's zip lists its info file before its archive, so the rescan could fire halfway through an install and delete the mod.
The game name Almost every published mod says it's for The_Walking_Dead_Definitive_Edition, which wasn't in the launcher's game list. The first mod got through because the check was skipped when nothing was installed yet. Every mod after it was rejected.
macOS junk One mod's zip has __MACOSX/._* files. The old launcher picked the last .json in the zip, which was one of those, so adding the mod failed.
Flattened paths Mods may list files in subfolders. The old launcher dropped the folders, then counted the files as missing and deleted the mod at startup.
The new one has no watcher, stages every install in a temporary folder before touching anything, flags missing files instead of deleting them, and skips junk.
Testing on a real install # First run on Windows, pointed at my Steam install I wrote the first version and tested it on Linux. When I pulled the branch onto my Windows PC and ran it against my real Steam install, two things showed up:
A test compared a path built with / against the \ path Windows returns. Saving settings failed now and then with “access denied”. Antivirus, the search indexer and sync tools like Syncthing open a newly written file for a moment, and Windows won’t replace a file while it’s open. In a loop of 2000 back-to-back saves, 174 failed. File moves and deletes now retry for up to about 0.4 seconds, and the same loop runs clean. Installing my own rewind mod also showed the old launcher copying every file in a zip into the game folder, including my install scripts and README. Now only the files a mod’s info json lists are installed, plus any archive or resource file it forgot to list, so older sloppy mods still work.
Load order you can drag # The game decides which mod wins a shared file by the priority in each mod’s _resdesc_*.lua. The old launcher showed that number but couldn’t change it, because most of those files are encrypted and the code that handled them lived in the missing DLL.
I ported Telltale’s Blowfish variant from ttarchext into C#. It’s standard Blowfish with a few P-array entries swapped and one S-box entry byte-swapped. Re-saving a file that ttarchext encrypted gives back its exact bytes, and every one of the 184 descriptors in my install decrypts.
Now the list is the load order. Drag a mod up or down, or use Move up and Move down in its right-click menu, and the launcher rewrites set.priority in the mod’s files so the game agrees. The numbers the mods already use get handed out again in the new order. The priority in a mod’s info json is treated as the author’s suggestion, and updating a mod keeps the place you gave it.
Swapping Season 2 Rewind and Graphic Black Disabler back and forth through the launcher, ttarchext read the new priorities straight out of the encrypted files each time.
Getting it # The 0.7.0 release has a Windows zip and a Linux tarball. Both are self-contained, so there’s nothing else to install. The work is also open as a pull request on my fork.
title: Rebuilding the Telltale Mod Launcher

content:
In the original release of The Walking Dead Season Two you could open an episode, pick any chapter you had already played, and rewind your save to that point. That is how I replay choices.
The Telltale Definitive Series bundles all four seasons plus Michonne into one game. Seasons 1, 3, 4 and Michonne still have a rewind menu. Season 2 doesn’t. Open an episode and all you get is Restart Episode.
So I went looking for the difference between the two releases.
Source and release on GitHub
Getting into the archives # Both games keep everything in .ttarch2 archives. They’re encrypted with a modified Blowfish and compressed, so grepping 46 GB of them for “rewind” goes nowhere. ttarchext by Luigi Auriemma handles both games, so I extracted the menu and script archives from each install and compared them.
The Season 2 menu in the Definitive Series is almost a copy of the original. Same scripts, same text, even the per-chapter thumbnail textures are still there. The rewind strings are still in the English text database:
REWIND BRANCH will allow you to replay this scene by creating a new save file, whereas REWIND will erase your currently selected save file back to this Chapter? To rewind this chapter, please choose a save file to copy the data. So the feature wasn’t removed. Something was hiding it.
Reading compiled Lua # The menus are written in Lua, shipped as compiled bytecode. The Definitive Series uses Lua 5.2 with 4-byte floats. The original Season Two uses Lua 5.1 with Telltale’s own shuffled opcode numbers, which makes it painful to read directly, but its string constants are enough to compare against.
I wrote a small disassembler in Python, pointed it at Menu_chapters.lua from the Definitive Series, and found this:
==== Menu_Chapters_RewindIsSupported lines 1054-1056 0 LOADBOOL R0 := False 1 RETURN return R0.. (1) A function that only returns false. It doesn’t exist in the original game. The chapter list only builds a panel for each autosave when this returns true, so in the Definitive Series the list is never built.
Two more changes went with it:
Original Season Two Definitive Series Chapter list Built for every autosave Gated behind RewindIsSupported(), which returns false Picking a chapter “Rewind” popup, then pick a save slot to rewind “Restart Episode” popup Button label navhelp_rewind navhelp_restart Everything the feature needs further down, like the save-slot rewind code and SaveLoad_Revert, is still there and untouched. Only this one script needed fixing.
Patching bytecode # I didn’t want to decompile and recompile the whole script, so I wrote a Lua 5.2 bytecode reader and writer that round-trips Telltale’s files byte for byte. Before changing anything I checked it against six different game scripts. Every one came back identical.
Then the patch is three small edits:
RewindIsSupported returns true. The popup goes back to the rewind text and calls Menu_Chapters_Replay(), which opens the save-slot picker like the original. The button label goes back to navhelp_rewind. The disassembly diff is short:
- 3 LOADK R1 := 'popup_restart_header' - 4 LOADK R2 := 'popup_restart_message' - 5 LOADK R3 := 'Menu_Chapters_NewStart()' - 6 CALL R0(3 args, 0 results) + 3 LOADK R1 := 'popup_rewind_header' + 4 LOADK R2 := 'popup_rewind_message' + 5 LOADK R3 := 'Menu_Chapters_Replay()' + 6 LOADK R4 := 'label_ok' + 7 CALL R0(4 args, 0 results) ... - 0 LOADBOOL R0 := False + 0 LOADBOOL R0 := True ... - 406 LOADK R4 := 'navhelp_restart' + 406 LOADK R4 := 'navhelp_rewind' Loading it without touching the game # I didn’t want to repack Telltale’s 800 KB menu archive. The engine has a cleaner way in.
At startup it runs every _resdesc_50_*.lua file in the Archives folder. Each one registers a set of archives with a priority. When two sets have a file with the same name, the higher priority wins. Telltale used exactly this for their own PC patches, at priority 400 over the stock 62.
So the mod is two files:
WDC_pc_Mod_S2Rewind_data.ttarch2, holding only the patched Menu_chapters.lua _resdesc_50_Mod_S2Rewind.lua, which registers it at priority 700 under the Season 2 menu local set = {} set.name = "Mod_S2Rewind" set.logicalDestination = "<MenuSeason2>" set.priority = 700 set.gameDataArchives = { _currentDirectory .. "WDC_pc_Mod_S2Rewind_data.ttarch2" } RegisterSetDescription(set) The descriptor has to be encrypted the same way the game’s own are, with an ESC LEo marker in front. To check that, I decrypted Telltale’s own patch descriptor, encrypted it again, and compared: the header matched the game’s file and decrypting it gave back the original text.
Nothing in the game is modified. Delete the two files and it’s stock again, and Steam’s file check leaves them alone because they’re additions, not replacements.
Testing it # Rewinding deletes the saves after the chapter you pick, same as the original game. Before trying it I copied my Season 2 save slot into an empty slot and tested on the copy. The chapter panels came back, Rewind showed up, and it worked.
The build script doesn’t ship any of Telltale’s files. It pulls the stock script out of your own install, patches it, packs it, then extracts and decrypts the result again to check both round trips.
Season 2 Rewind installed through the launcher With the mod launcher # The mod also works with the Telltale Mod Launcher, which is how it’s installed here.
Version 1.0.1 only renamed its info file to modinfo_season2_rewind.json so it’s obvious in the Archives folder which mod it belongs to.
title: Bringing Chapter Rewind Back to Season 2

content:
Steam Cloud is great when a game has it. Plenty don’t, including a lot of the older games I play on the Deck. I already run Syncthing on the Deck and my PC, but adding a game meant going to Desktop Mode, finding the save folder somewhere inside a Proton prefix, and setting up the share by hand in Syncthing’s web UI. For every game.
SyncDeck does that from the Quick Access Menu.
Source and releases on GitHub
What it does # The SyncDeck panel in the Quick Access Menu Lists the installed Steam games, across every library including SD cards, by reading Steam’s appmanifest files. Finds where each game keeps its saves and shows the best match. It looks in the Proton prefix (Saved Games, Documents/My Games, publisher folders under AppData), the Linux XDG folders, and save/ folders inside the install. You confirm before anything is created. Creates the Syncthing folder, shares it with the devices you pick, and turns on versioning so a bad sync can be undone. Shows each game’s state: up to date, syncing, scanning, waiting for the PC to accept, paused, or an error. Picks up Syncthing folders you made by hand and shows them as synced, without ever deleting them. Can install a user systemd unit so Syncthing starts at login, even in Gaming Mode. Games that already have Steam Cloud are hidden by default, since Steam handles those.
The PC side # By default, adding a game makes the PC’s Syncthing show a “the Deck wants to share a folder” notice, and you accept it there. While it waits, SyncDeck shows the matching Windows path so you know where to point it.
There’s also an optional mode where SyncDeck creates the folder on the PC itself through Syncthing’s REST API, in the right place:
Proton prefix saves Go to the same place in your Windows profile, like ~\Documents\My Games\.... If the game is installed on the PC too, the two merge.
Saves in the install folder Go to the game's real install folder on the PC. SyncDeck finds it by checking the PC's usual Steam library locations.
Everything else Anything with no Windows equivalent goes under ~\SyncDeck\<Game> as a backup.
That mode needs the PC’s Syncthing API key, and typing a 32-character key on the Deck’s on-screen keyboard is miserable. So you can drop the key into a text file in any folder the Deck already syncs. It arrives on the Deck by itself, and one button reads it in and deletes the file.
Building it # Decky plugins have a Python backend and a React front end in TypeScript. The backend does all the file system and Syncthing work. The front end is the panel in the screenshot.
The first public release was 1.0.0 on September 16. Most of what followed came from actually using it: SD card awareness, relocating a folder when a game’s saves move, forgetting games that are gone, and the PC auto-add mode. It’s at 1.4.2 now, with CI and a release workflow on GitHub.
title: SyncDeck: Steam Deck Saves to My PC with Syncthing

content:
Inferno Nihongo turns real Japanese, like manga, light novels and screenshots, into study material. Point it at a page, read it with help, and the words you looked up come back for review. No generic decks: you review the words you actually met.
It’s live at japan.infernokun.com, free to try while it’s in evaluation.
Scan # Reviewing a scan: green words are included Photograph any page # Upload a photo, a screenshot, a PDF or a CBZ. OCR finds the text, including vertical text, rotated pages and speech bubbles, and rebuilds it as real text with the reading order fixed.
See what it found # Real scans are messy, so before anything is saved every word is boxed on the image. Drop false positives, fix a reading, and tune how eagerly nearby boxes merge into one speech bubble. Furigana is left out by default, because those little reading aids get swept into the text and ruin it.
Read # Once a page is in your library, every speech bubble it found gets a marker.
Tap a marker and the bubble opens as real text, with furigana over the kanji Open as many as you like and read the page that way The word card Tap any word # A tap shows the reading, meanings, the conjugation broken down (dictionary form plus passive plus past, and so on), JLPT level, frequency rank, WaniKani progress, the kanji with their readings and parts, example sentences, and where else in your library the word shows up.
Words you’ve saved are underlined green. Words saved from a different series show orange, so your vocabulary follows you from book to book.
Reading a novel page by page Novels too # Text-heavy pages get a page reader instead, with furigana above only the kanji you don’t know yet.
The pages down the side are photos of the physical book, each one turned into text you can tap.
Remember # A page from the getting-started book Review what you met # Saved words go into spaced-repetition review. If you already know a word you can mark it known right from the reader.
A built-in getting-started book walks through all of this, including how a scan is reviewed.
How it’s built # It’s four services, all in Docker:
Web: Angular 22 with TypeScript and SCSS. API: Spring Boot 3.5 on Java 25, with PostgreSQL and Redis. The Japanese analysis lives in its own Gradle module, hibana (火花, “spark”): the tokenizer, bundled JMdict, JMnedict, KANJIDIC2 and Tanaka data, and the dictionary ranking, with no database, HTTP or auth in it. Translate: a Python FastAPI service for OCR, furigana, translation, and rendering pages out of PDFs and CBZs. Mobile: a Flutter app for Android and iOS on the same API, with an offline mode. My own GitLab builds and tests everything and pushes the images to my own registry. Next to test coverage for each service, the pipeline reports a reader accuracy score and an answer accuracy score, so a change that makes either one worse shows up before it ships.
title: Inferno Nihongo: Learning Japanese from the Manga I'm Already Reading

content:
Inferno Comics tracks my comic collection: what I own, what I’m missing, and what’s coming out. Most of it is DC, with some Marvel and manga. The point of it is that adding comics is mostly taking photos instead of typing in every issue.
Adding comics # Searching Comic Vine Adding a series # Series come from Comic Vine. Search, tick the results you want, and they’re added with their issue lists, covers and dates. Several results can also be combined into one series.
A photo of a bagged comic next to the cover it matched Adding issues by photo # Take photos of your comics, upload them, and the recognition service compares each photo against the covers of every issue in the series.
It uses OpenCV’s AKAZE feature matching, which works from distinctive points in the image rather than the whole picture, so a comic still in its bag and photographed on a table can be matched. Each result comes with a confidence score.
Processing status A whole stack at once # With a whole stack of photos you get a bulk review. High-confidence matches can be accepted in one go, and the rest you check by hand.
Matching runs in the background, and you can watch each job’s progress.
Your collection # My copies of Absolute Wonder Woman, with read status Each series page shows the issues you own with their covers and release dates. Every issue carries its condition grade and whether you’ve read it, and the next unread issue is marked so you know where to pick up.
Tracking the gaps # With the issue lists from Comic Vine, the app knows what you don’t have. The Missing page lists every gap by series.
Series get reverified every so often, and new issues that turn up land on the Releases page, grouped by month. The Stats page has the overall picture. Right now that’s 78 series and 610 issues across 7 publishers.
New releases I don't have yet Collection stats How it’s built # Web: Angular 21 with NgRx, AG Grid and Angular Material. API: Spring Boot 3.5 on Java 25, with PostgreSQL 17 and Redis. Long jobs report progress over server-sent events. Recognition: a Python Flask service using OpenCV, with a SQLite cache. Extras: Comic Vine for metadata, an AI model through Groq for series descriptions, and Nextcloud for syncing files. There’s also an Android app, and a tool that imports the Grand Comics Database for extra series and issue data. Each service is its own Docker image, built by my GitLab and published to Docker Hub.
title: Inferno Comics: A Collection Tracker That Recognizes Covers

content:
Project TTG is a work-in-progress game in Unreal Engine, built around a Clementine model from Telltale’s The Walking Dead. It borrows from two places: the point and click style of Telltale’s adventures, and the third-person feel of the Resident Evil remakes.
It’s purely for learning, with no plans for any kind of release. Everything here lives in a grey-box test level, because the point is getting the systems right, not content.
Gameplay # Aiming with the flashlight Third-person # From the Resident Evil remakes it takes the camera over the shoulder, a flashlight that matters, and careful movement. In a full game that style also means limited resources and puzzles built into the environment.
Gameplay Blueprint Blueprints # The gameplay logic is built in Blueprints, Unreal’s visual scripting. Events, functions and interactions with the world are all wired up there, which makes it quick to try an idea without writing C++ first.
Animation # Control Rig Control Rig # The character animation goes through Control Rig, Unreal’s node-based tool for building skeletal controls and animating them procedurally. It lets the character react to the world instead of only playing back canned animations.
Control Rig Blueprint Control Rig Blueprints # Control Rig setups can be packaged as Control Rig Blueprints, so the same setup can be reused and configured across characters.
Clementine in the engine The Clementine model # Getting Clementine into Unreal meant setting up the model, rigging it, and getting it animating. With Control Rig driving her, I could clone existing animations and adjust them instead of animating everything from scratch.
title: Project TTG: A Telltale-Style Game in Unreal

content:
I'm Javoris. Online I go by InfernoKun.
I build the tools I want to use and then keep going until they hold up. Most of what I make falls into a few buckets:
Self-hosted web apps Angular front ends, Spring Boot APIs, Python services for the heavy lifting, all in Docker and built by my own GitLab.
Game mods and modding tools Mostly Telltale's games, where I take apart archives and Lua bytecode to change how they behave.
Steam Deck and Linux bits Small plugins that fix something that annoyed me.
Game dev experiments Unreal and Unity projects I use to learn animation, cameras and gameplay systems.
This site is where I write those projects up: why I started them, how they work, and what broke along the way.
My code is on GitHub.
